subject: astronomy

moments.title: Cannon classifies 350,000 stars
moments.who: Annie Jump Cannon, Harvard College Observatory
moments.body: Cannon, working among the 'Harvard Computers' (a team of women paid 25 cents an hour to analyse stellar spectra under Edward Pickering), refines the spectral classification system to OBAFGKM — by temperature, not by hydrogen-line strength as earlier classifications had assumed. She personally classifies over 350,000 stars. The Henry Draper Catalogue (1918-24) becomes the standard.
moments.takeaway: The classification system used in every modern astronomy textbook was built by one woman over a quarter-century, surrounded by colleagues paid less than typists.

moments.title: Leavitt's period-luminosity law
moments.who: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, Harvard College Observatory
moments.body: Leavitt, another Harvard Computer, discovers that Cepheid variable stars have a period-luminosity relationship: brighter Cepheids pulse more slowly. This means a Cepheid's brightness can be calibrated from its period, making them 'standard candles' for measuring distance.
moments.takeaway: Leavitt's law later allowed Hubble to measure that Andromeda was outside the Milky Way and the universe was expanding. She died of cancer in 1921 at 53, before her work transformed cosmology.

now.title: Spectroscopy today
now.body: OBAFGKM classification is universal; the mnemonic 'Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy Kiss Me' has its own awkward history. Spectral classification has been extended (L, T, Y for brown dwarfs). Cepheid standard candles remain a key rung of the distance ladder. The Annie Jump Cannon Award and the Henrietta Swan Leavitt Award honour their namesakes.
now.open_questions: How are the spectra of the very earliest stars (Population III) different? JWST is starting to answer.

reflection: The Harvard Computers — Cannon, Leavitt, Williamina Fleming, Antonia Maury — produced a generation of foundational astronomy. They were called 'Pickering's Harem' at the time. Dava Sobel's 'The Glass Universe' (2016) restored their story.
